metrics.label: WTI crude

metrics.label: Henry Hub gas

metrics.label: Coal API2 (ARA)

metrics.label: Heating oil / gasoil

metrics.label: RBOB gasoline

metrics.label: Dry bulk ETF (BDRY)

metrics.blurb: An ETF holding tanker freight futures. A rough daily read on tanker sentiment.

metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Baltic Dry Index
metrics.blurb: The Baltic Exchange's headline dry bulk freight index. Published late afternoon London time, so a morning brief shows the previous session.

metrics.label: VLSFO Singapore
metrics.blurb: Price of the main low-sulphur marine fuel at the world's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Rotterdam
metrics.blurb: The same fuel in Europe's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Fujairah
metrics.blurb: The Middle East bunker hub, where most VLCC voyages refuel.

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent
metrics.blurb: Roughly what a refinery makes turning a barrel of crude into diesel. Computed as the gasoil price converted to barrels minus Brent. Fat margins make refineries run hard, which creates product tanker cargo.

metrics.label: Brent–WTI spread
metrics.blurb: How much more Brent costs than WTI. A wide gap makes exporting US crude profitable, which means more long-haul cargoes and stronger tanker demand.

brief.text:
The clearest thing in today's data is a split between crude and bunkers. Brent crude, the main global oil benchmark, was observed today at $99.86 a barrel, up $1.57 (+1.6%), and WTI at $91.61, up $1.09 (+1.2%). Yet VLSFO — very low sulphur fuel oil, the standard marine fuel you cost into a voyage — fell in all four bunker ports today: Singapore $849.50 a tonne, down $52.00 (-5.8%), Fujairah $851.50, down $56.00 (-6.2%), Rotterdam $732.00, down $15.00 (-2.0%) and Houston $754.00, down $10.00 (-1.3%). Cheaper bunkers lower the cost side of any voyage calculation, and the Asia/Middle East ports fell far harder than the Atlantic ones. Nothing in today's headlines explains either the crude rise or the bunker fall, so treat both as unexplained by this data.

Elsewhere in today's figures, RBOB gasoline was $2.81 a gallon (+1.8%) and gasoil $4.38 (+0.7%), with Henry Hub US gas at $3.00/mmBtu (+1.6%). The diesel crack against Brent stood at $84.27 a barrel and the Brent–WTI spread at $8.25, both today, with no change figure given. No freight benchmark has refreshed today. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks bulk carrier earnings, was 2,740 points on Thursday 5 November, up 46 (+1.7%), and the dry bulk ETF BDRY was $13.02 the same day, up 3.3%, while the tanker ETF BWET was $669.89, down 3.1%. Tanker TCEs — time charter equivalent, the daily earnings a voyage converts to — are old: VLCC TD3C was $1,345,710 a day on Sunday 1 November, and Suezmax TD20 $406,769 a day on Sunday 25 October.

Among running stories, Hormuz remains live: today's data reports a Hormuz tanker strike via UKMTO alongside LPG carriers being dropped from Iran's non-compliance list, and South Korea plans to move naval assets closer to the strait. Sanctions enforcement widened today, with the US State Department sanctioning five ships and two people over Cuba's oil shipping network, and seven sanctioned tankers reported spoofing AIS positions to hide Novorossiysk voyages. Black Sea drone attacks, Russian diesel export restrictions and the US West Coast port labour standoff had no news today and are unchanged.

Watch two things. First, whether tanker TCEs refresh, since the most recent prints are five and ten sessions old and cannot tell you anything about this week. Second, whether AIS spoofing and the Cuba designations trigger more documentation checks on fixtures.

storylines.title: Direct attacks on ships in Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into November, including a VLCC whose engine room was struck in Omani waters. Today UKMTO is reported to have logged a further tanker strike.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on hulls raise war-risk premiums and crew-safety objections for Arabian Gulf liftings, shrinking the pool of willing owners and supporting crude and product tanker earnings.
storylines.latest: A Hormuz tanker strike reported by UKMTO, and South Korea said it wants to deploy naval assets closer to the strait.

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Strait of Hormuz traffic rose in October to its highest monthly level since July, supported by dry bulk and LNG movements even as VLCC traffic declined. Red Sea traffic also rose and Arabian Gulf waiting remains elevated.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: The US sanctioned a network running fraudulent ship registries and false-flag services for Iranian shadow fleet vessels, and today expanded sanctions to five ships and two people tied to Cuba's oil shipping network. Separately, seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found manipulating AIS to disguise Novorossiysk voyages.
storylines.why_it_matters: Registry fraud and AIS spoofing force charterers, insurers and class societies to re-verify documentation and positions, and can push sanctioned tonnage out of mainstream trades, tightening compliant tanker supply.
storylines.latest: US State Department sanctioned five ships and two people over Cuban oil shipping; seven sanctioned tankers reported spoofing AIS near the Bosphorus; US-sanctioned LPG carriers removed from Iran's PGSA non-compliance list.

storylines.title: Drone attacks on shipping in the western Black Sea
storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, the latest in a series of strikes in the western Black Sea.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings from the region and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling there.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia agreement on supplying extra diesel to the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a general ban on most diesel exports until the end of January, with some volumes still allowed to flow.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment patterns.

storylines.title: Port labour disruption in the US and Europe
storylines.what: A contract standoff involving 250 security workers threatens to freeze operations across Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals after a 4 November deadline extension, while dockworkers struck across Europe and beyond over arms shipments.
storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Strait of Hormuz traffic rose in October to its highest monthly level since July, supported by dry bulk and LNG movements even as VLCC traffic declined. Red Sea traffic also rose and Arabian Gulf waiting remains elevated.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: The US sanctioned a network running fraudulent ship registries and false-flag services for Iranian shadow fleet vessels, and today expanded sanctions to five ships and two people tied to Cuba's oil shipping network. Separately, seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found manipulating AIS to disguise Novorossiysk voyages.
storylines.why_it_matters: Registry fraud and AIS spoofing force charterers, insurers and class societies to re-verify documentation and positions, and can push sanctioned tonnage out of mainstream trades, tightening compliant tanker supply.
storylines.latest: US State Department sanctioned five ships and two people over Cuban oil shipping; seven sanctioned tankers reported spoofing AIS near the Bosphorus; US-sanctioned LPG carriers removed from Iran's PGSA non-compliance list.
sources: U.S. State Department Expands Sanctions on Cuban Shipping
Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
US-sanctioned ships dropped from Iran's PGSA blacklist

storylines.title: Drone attacks on shipping in the western Black Sea
storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, the latest in a series of strikes in the western Black Sea.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings from the region and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling there.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia agreement on supplying extra diesel to the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a general ban on most diesel exports until the end of January, with some volumes still allowed to flow.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment patterns.

storylines.title: Port labour disruption in the US and Europe
storylines.what: A contract standoff involving 250 security workers threatens to freeze operations across Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals after a 4 November deadline extension, while dockworkers struck across Europe and beyond over arms shipments.
storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.
